subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: 9.6 Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics

questions.q: A copper block rests on a laboratory bench at room temperature. Which of the following makes up the internal energy of the block?
options: The kinetic energy of its vibrating atoms, without any potential energy of their arrangement
The heat stored in the block, which it gives out when it is placed next to a colder object
The kinetic energy of its vibrating atoms plus the potential energy of their arrangement
The block's gravitational potential energy on the bench plus the kinetic energy of the whole block
optionWhy: A student who thinks internal energy is only the random kinetic energy of the particles picks this. That is true of an ideal gas, whose atoms exert no conservative forces on one another, but the atoms of a solid are held in place by such forces, so the block's internal energy also includes the potential energy of their arrangement.

A student who thinks of heat as something an object contains picks this. Heating is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; it is not stored as heat. What the block contains is internal energy, the kinetic and potential energy of its atoms, which heating or cooling can change.

Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energies of the objects that make up the system (here, copper atoms vibrating about their positions) and the potential energy of their configuration, which comes from the forces the atoms exert on one another.

A student who counts the energy of the block as a whole picks this. The gravitational potential energy belongs to the block–Earth system and depends on the block's position, and the kinetic energy of the whole block depends on the motion of its center of mass; neither is internal energy, which concerns the atoms' motion and arrangement relative to one another.
questions.explain: Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energies of the objects that make up the system (here, copper atoms vibrating about their positions) and the potential energy of their configuration, which comes from the forces the atoms exert on one another.

questions.q: A sealed container of ideal gas rests on a level table. The container is heated, and the temperature of the gas increases. Which statement describes the gas and the container after the heating?
options: The container starts to move, as its gas has gained kinetic energy.
The gas atoms keep their average speed, but the gas now holds more heat.
The gas atoms move faster on average, and the container stays at rest.
The container now weighs less, as the gas in it is heated and hot gas rises.
optionWhy: A student who thinks that the kinetic energy gained by the atoms must appear as motion of the whole object picks this. The atoms move in random directions, so their extra kinetic energy is internal energy; with no net external horizontal force, the center of mass stays at rest.

A student who thinks heat is a substance stored alongside the atoms picks this. The energy transferred by heating becomes internal energy, which for an ideal gas is the kinetic energy of its atoms, so their average speed must increase as the temperature rises.

Heating increases the internal energy of the gas, which for an ideal gas is the kinetic energy of its atoms moving randomly relative to one another: a higher temperature means a greater average kinetic energy. The random motions add to zero net momentum, so the center of mass of the gas and container stays at rest.

A student who thinks heated gas weighs less because hot air rises picks this. Hot air rises through cooler air because it is less dense; the sealed container holds the same mass of gas before and after heating, so its weight is unchanged.
questions.explain: Heating increases the internal energy of the gas, which for an ideal gas is the kinetic energy of its atoms moving randomly relative to one another: a higher temperature means a greater average kinetic energy. The random motions add to zero net momentum, so the center of mass of the gas and container stays at rest.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg copper block at 80°C and a 1.0 kg copper block at 20°C are placed in contact inside an insulated box, and the two blocks form an isolated system. They reach the same final temperature. Which statement about the energy of the blocks is correct?
options: The blocks' total energy has fallen, as some was used up in the transfer.
The total energy of the two blocks is the same afterward as it was beforehand.
The two blocks end with equal internal energies, as they have equal temperatures.
The cold block keeps the same energy, and its cold passes into the hot block.
optionWhy: A student who thinks energy is used up when it is transferred picks this. Energy is conserved: in an isolated system none can be lost, so all of the energy lost by the hotter block is gained by the colder block.

The two blocks form an isolated system, so their total energy is constant. Energy is transferred from the hotter block to the colder one until their temperatures are equal: the internal energy lost by the 2.0 kg block equals the internal energy gained by the 1.0 kg block.

A student who thinks equal temperatures mean equal internal energies picks this. Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy per atom; the 2.0 kg block has twice as many atoms at the same final temperature, so it has more internal energy.

A student who thinks of cold as something that flows picks this. Energy is transferred from the hotter block to the colder block; the colder block's temperature rises because its internal energy increases.
questions.explain: The two blocks form an isolated system, so their total energy is constant. Energy is transferred from the hotter block to the colder one until their temperatures are equal: the internal energy lost by the 2.0 kg block equals the internal energy gained by the 1.0 kg block.

questions.q: A gas in a cylinder is compressed by a piston. During the compression, 250 J of work is done on the gas, and 400 J of energy is transferred from the gas to its surroundings by cooling. What is the change in the internal energy of the gas?
optionWhy: ΔU = Q + W. The work done on the gas is W = +250 J, and energy leaving by cooling makes Q = −400 J. ΔU = −400 J + 250 J = −150 J: the gas loses more energy by cooling than it gains as work.
A student who takes W as the work done by the gas picks this: W = −250 J gives ΔU = −400 J − 250 J = −650 J. In ΔU = Q + W, W is the work done on the gas, +250 J for a compression.
A student who adds the two energy transfers without signs picks this: 400 J + 250 J = 650 J. Energy leaving the gas by cooling makes Q negative, −400 J.
A student who counts only the energy transferred by cooling picks this. The 250 J of work done on the gas is also a transfer of energy into it, which makes up part of the 400 J lost.
questions.explain: ΔU = Q + W. The work done on the gas is W = +250 J, and energy leaving by cooling makes Q = −400 J. ΔU = −400 J + 250 J = −150 J: the gas loses more energy by cooling than it gains as work.
questions.working: ΔU = Q + W. W = +250 J (work done on the gas); Q = −400 J (energy leaves by cooling). ΔU = −400 J + 250 J = −150 J.

questions.q: A sample of ideal gas in a cylinder expands slowly, pushing a piston outward, while its temperature is kept constant. How does the internal energy U_f of the gas at the end of the expansion compare with its internal energy U_i at the start?
options: U_f > U_i, since with its atoms farther apart the gas stores more potential energy
U_f < U_i, since the gas does work on the piston and loses that much internal energy
They cannot be compared without first knowing how much energy was added to the gas by heating
U_f = U_i, since spacing stores no energy and the atoms' average kinetic energy is unchanged
optionWhy: A student who thinks an ideal gas stores potential energy in the spacing of its atoms picks this. Ideal-gas atoms exert no conservative forces on one another, so moving them apart changes no potential energy; with T constant, U is unchanged.

A student who counts only the work picks this. The gas does transfer energy out as work, but an equal amount is transferred in by heating, which is what keeps its temperature constant: ΔU = Q + W = 0.

A student who thinks internal energy depends on the process rather than on the state picks this. For a fixed amount of ideal gas, U = (3/2)nRT depends only on the temperature, which is the same at the start and at the end, so no value of Q is needed.

The atoms of an ideal gas exert no conservative forces on one another, so the gas has no internal potential energy and the change in their spacing does not matter. Its internal energy is the kinetic energy of its atoms, which for a fixed amount of gas depends only on the temperature; T is constant, so U_f = U_i. (The energy transferred in by heating equals the energy transferred out as work.)
questions.explain: The atoms of an ideal gas exert no conservative forces on one another, so the gas has no internal potential energy and the change in their spacing does not matter. Its internal energy is the kinetic energy of its atoms, which for a fixed amount of gas depends only on the temperature; T is constant, so U_f = U_i. (The energy transferred in by heating equals the energy transferred out as work.)

questions.q: A sealed, rigid steel container holds an ideal monatomic gas at 27°C, and the internal energy of the gas is U₀. The gas is heated until its temperature is 327°C. What is the internal energy of the gas now?
optionWhy: For a fixed amount of ideal monatomic gas, U = (3/2)nRT is proportional to the absolute temperature. The temperature rises from 27 + 273 = 300 K to 327 + 273 = 600 K, so the internal energy doubles.
A student who uses the Celsius temperatures picks this: 327/27 ≈ 12.1. U = (3/2)nRT needs absolute temperatures, and 300 K to 600 K is a factor of 2.

A student who uses the factor for the rms speed picks this: v_rms is proportional to √T, so it increases by √2 ≈ 1.41. The internal energy is the sum of the atoms' kinetic energies, which is proportional to T itself, so it doubles.

A student who thinks internal energy changes only when work is done picks this, since no work is done in a rigid container. Energy is transferred to the gas by heating, so ΔU = Q + W = Q > 0, and the internal energy doubles.
questions.explain: For a fixed amount of ideal monatomic gas, U = (3/2)nRT is proportional to the absolute temperature. The temperature rises from 27 + 273 = 300 K to 327 + 273 = 600 K, so the internal energy doubles.
questions.working: U = (3/2)nRT with T in kelvins; n is fixed. T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K, T₂ = 327 + 273 = 600 K. U/U₀ = 600 K/300 K = 2.00, so U = 2.00U₀. (Celsius ratio 327/27 ≈ 12.1; √2 ≈ 1.41 is the factor for v_rms; 1.00U₀ ignores the heating.)

questions.q: A cylinder holds 0.40 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 77°C. What is the internal energy of the gas? Use R = 8.31 J/(mol·K).
optionWhy: A student who uses nRT as the internal energy picks this: (0.40)(8.31)(350) = 1.2 × 10³ J. nRT equals PV; the internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas is (3/2)nRT.

A student who thinks U depends only on the temperature, not on the amount of gas, picks this: (3/2)(8.31)(350) = 4.4 × 10³ J, the internal energy of one mole. The cylinder holds 0.40 mol, so U is 0.40 times as great.
A student who uses the Celsius temperature picks this: (3/2)(0.40)(8.31)(77) = 3.8 × 10² J. The equation needs the absolute temperature, 350 K.
The internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas is U = (3/2)nRT, with T in kelvins: T = 77 + 273 = 350 K. U = (3/2)(0.40 mol)(8.31 J/(mol·K))(350 K) = 1.7 × 10³ J.
questions.explain: The internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas is U = (3/2)nRT, with T in kelvins: T = 77 + 273 = 350 K. U = (3/2)(0.40 mol)(8.31 J/(mol·K))(350 K) = 1.7 × 10³ J.

questions.q: The outlet of a bicycle pump is blocked, and the frictionless piston is pushed in quickly, compressing the air inside. The piston, the cylinder and the air start at the same temperature. Model the air as an ideal gas. The temperature of the air rises. Which explanation is correct?
options: The piston does work on the air, transferring energy that raises its internal energy.
The heat already in the air is squeezed into a smaller volume, so the air is hotter.
Energy is transferred to the air by heating, as heating is what raises temperature.
The air's pressure rises, and a higher pressure in itself makes a gas hotter.
optionWhy: The first law is conservation of energy: ΔU = Q + W. In the quick compression the piston does positive work on the air, W > 0, and there is almost no time for energy to leave by cooling, so the internal energy of the air, and with it the temperature, increases.

A student who thinks of heat as a substance that can be concentrated picks this. The air does not contain heat; its internal energy increases because work is done on it, so the temperature rise comes from new energy, not the same energy in less space.

A student who thinks only heating can raise a gas's internal energy or temperature picks this. Nothing in contact with the air is hotter than it, so there is no heating; the energy comes from the work done by the piston.

A student who thinks temperature follows pressure alone picks this. A slow compression at constant temperature also raises the pressure; what raises the temperature here is the work done on the air with no time for cooling.
questions.explain: The first law is conservation of energy: ΔU = Q + W. In the quick compression the piston does positive work on the air, W > 0, and there is almost no time for energy to leave by cooling, so the internal energy of the air, and with it the temperature, increases.

questions.q: A block of mass m slides across a rough, level floor, and its speed decreases from v to v/2. Consider the system of the block and the floor, and assume that no energy is transferred between this system and its surroundings, so that it is isolated. By how much does the internal energy of the system increase while the speed decreases?
optionWhy: A student who drops the ½ from the kinetic energy picks this: mv² − m(v/2)² = (3/4)mv². With K = (1/2)mv², the decrease is (1/2)mv² − (1/8)mv² = (3/8)mv².
A student who squares the change in speed picks this: (1/2)m(v − v/2)² = (1/8)mv². Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed, so each kinetic energy must be found before subtracting.

The system is isolated, so its total energy is constant. The floor is level, so only kinetic energy and internal energy change: the kinetic energy falls from (1/2)mv² to (1/2)m(v/2)² = (1/8)mv², a decrease of (3/8)mv², and the internal energy of the block and floor (the motion and arrangement of their atoms at the rubbing surfaces) increases by that amount.

A student who takes the whole initial kinetic energy as the increase in internal energy picks this. The block is still moving at v/2, so it keeps (1/8)mv² of kinetic energy; only the decrease, (3/8)mv², becomes internal energy.
questions.explain: The system is isolated, so its total energy is constant. The floor is level, so only kinetic energy and internal energy change: the kinetic energy falls from (1/2)mv² to (1/2)m(v/2)² = (1/8)mv², a decrease of (3/8)mv², and the internal energy of the block and floor (the motion and arrangement of their atoms at the rubbing surfaces) increases by that amount.
questions.working: Isolated system, level floor: ΔK + ΔU_int = 0. ΔK = (1/2)m(v/2)² − (1/2)mv² = (1/8)mv² − (4/8)mv² = −(3/8)mv², so the internal energy increases by (3/8)mv². (Errors: dropping ½ gives (3/4)mv²; (1/2)m(Δv)² gives (1/8)mv²; the initial kinetic energy is (1/2)mv².)

questions.q: The P–V diagram shows a process in which a sample of ideal monatomic gas goes from state i to state f. During the process, 1.0 × 10³ J of energy is transferred to the gas by heating. What is the change in the internal energy of the gas?
optionWhy: A student who takes W as the work done by the gas, +4.0 × 10² J, picks this. In ΔU = Q + W, W is the work done on the gas, which is negative in an expansion.

The gas expands at constant pressure, so the work done on it is W = −PΔV = −(2.0 × 10⁵ Pa)(2.0 × 10⁻³ m³) = −4.0 × 10² J: the gas transfers energy to its surroundings as it pushes outward. ΔU = Q + W = 1.0 × 10³ J − 4.0 × 10² J = +6.0 × 10² J.

A student who thinks all of the energy transferred by heating stays in the gas picks this. As it expands, the gas transfers 4.0 × 10² J to its surroundings as work, so its internal energy increases by only 6.0 × 10² J.
A student who counts only the work picks this, leaving out the 1.0 × 10³ J transferred in by heating. Both transfers change the internal energy: ΔU = Q + W.
questions.explain: The gas expands at constant pressure, so the work done on it is W = −PΔV = −(2.0 × 10⁵ Pa)(2.0 × 10⁻³ m³) = −4.0 × 10² J: the gas transfers energy to its surroundings as it pushes outward. ΔU = Q + W = 1.0 × 10³ J − 4.0 × 10² J = +6.0 × 10² J.
questions.working: Graph: horizontal line at P = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa from V = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ (constant-pressure expansion). W = −PΔV = −(2.0 × 10⁵ Pa)(2.0 × 10⁻³ m³) = −4.0 × 10² J. ΔU = Q + W = 1.0 × 10³ J − 4.0 × 10² J = +6.0 × 10² J. (Check: for a monatomic ideal gas at constant pressure ΔU = (3/2)PΔV = 6.0 × 10² J and Q = (5/2)PΔV = 1.0 × 10³ J, consistent with the stem.)

questions.q: A 0.200 kg aluminum block is heated from 20.0°C to 60.0°C. The specific heat of aluminum is 900 J/(kg·K). How much energy is transferred to the block?
optionWhy: A student who puts the final temperature, 60.0°C, in place of the temperature change picks this: (0.200 kg)(900 J/(kg·K))(60.0) = 1.1 × 10⁴ J. Q = mcΔT needs the change, 40.0 K.
The temperature change is ΔT = 60.0°C − 20.0°C = 40.0 K; a change of one Celsius degree is a change of one kelvin. Q = mcΔT = (0.200 kg)(900 J/(kg·K))(40.0 K) = 7.2 × 10³ J.
A student who adds 273 to the temperature change picks this, using ΔT = 313 K. Adding 273 converts a temperature, not a difference: a rise of 40.0°C is a rise of 40.0 K.

A student who treats the specific heat as the energy needed to warm the whole block by 1 K picks this, leaving out the mass: (900 J/(kg·K))(40.0 K). Specific heat is energy per kilogram per kelvin, so it must be multiplied by the mass, 0.200 kg.
questions.explain: The temperature change is ΔT = 60.0°C − 20.0°C = 40.0 K; a change of one Celsius degree is a change of one kelvin. Q = mcΔT = (0.200 kg)(900 J/(kg·K))(40.0 K) = 7.2 × 10³ J.

questions.q: The specific heat of liquid water is about twice the specific heat of ice. Which statement best accounts for this difference?
options: Liquid water is denser than ice, so each kilogram of it contains more molecules.
Freezing changes how the molecules interact, so the energy per kilogram per kelvin changes.
Liquid water is warmer than ice, so it contains more heat to begin with.
Liquid water conducts energy better than ice, so it takes in more energy.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a denser material packs more molecules into each kilogram picks this. Density is mass per unit volume; a kilogram of ice and a kilogram of liquid water contain the same number of molecules, because every water molecule has the same mass.

Specific heat is an intrinsic property that depends on how a material's atoms or molecules are arranged and interact. Ice and liquid water are the same substance, but freezing changes the arrangement of the molecules and how they interact, so each phase has its own specific heat.

A student who thinks of heat as something an object contains picks this. Specific heat is the energy needed per kilogram per kelvin of temperature change, not energy stored in a sample, and ice and liquid water can both be at 0°C.

A student who treats thermal conductivity and specific heat as one property picks this. Conductivity describes how fast energy passes through a material; specific heat describes how much energy a kilogram needs per kelvin. In fact ice conducts better than liquid water.
questions.explain: Specific heat is an intrinsic property that depends on how a material's atoms or molecules are arranged and interact. Ice and liquid water are the same substance, but freezing changes the arrangement of the molecules and how they interact, so each phase has its own specific heat.

questions.q: A 0.300 kg iron block at 80.0°C is placed in 0.500 kg of water at 20.0°C in an insulated container, and the block and the water reach a common temperature. The specific heat of iron is 450 J/(kg·K), and the specific heat of water is 4180 J/(kg·K). Energy transfer to the container and the surroundings is negligible. What is the common temperature?
optionWhy: A student who takes the common temperature to be halfway between the starting temperatures picks this. That holds only when the two objects have equal values of mc; here the water's mc is about 15 times the iron's, so the common temperature is much closer to 20.0°C.

A student who weights the two temperatures by mass alone picks this, as if a kilogram of iron and a kilogram of water needed the same energy per kelvin. Their specific heats differ by a factor of more than 9, and the energy balance must include them.

A student who thinks the material with the greater specific heat changes temperature more picks this: in effect the two specific heats are swapped, so the water warms by about 51 K while the iron cools by only about 9 K. The reverse is true: water's large specific heat keeps its temperature change small.

The energy transferred from the iron equals the energy transferred to the water: (0.300 kg)(450 J/(kg·K))(80.0°C − T) = (0.500 kg)(4180 J/(kg·K))(T − 20.0°C), which gives T = 23.6°C. The water, with much the larger mc, changes temperature much less than the iron.
questions.explain: The energy transferred from the iron equals the energy transferred to the water: (0.300 kg)(450 J/(kg·K))(80.0°C − T) = (0.500 kg)(4180 J/(kg·K))(T − 20.0°C), which gives T = 23.6°C. The water, with much the larger mc, changes temperature much less than the iron.

questions.q: A copper rod, insulated along its sides, connects two reservoirs held at different temperatures, and energy is conducted along it at a steady rate. The rod is replaced by a copper rod of the same length but twice the diameter, and the temperature difference between the reservoirs is halved. By what factor does the rate of energy transfer along the rod change?
options: ×½
×⅛
optionWhy: A student who doubles the area when the diameter doubles picks this: 2 × ½ = 1. The area of a circle is πd²/4, so doubling the diameter makes it four times as great.

A student who thinks the rate does not depend on the rod's cross-sectional area picks this, counting only the halved temperature difference. A wider rod provides more paths for conduction: the rate is proportional to A.
Q/Δt = kAΔT/L. The cross-sectional area is proportional to the square of the diameter, so doubling the diameter makes the area 4 times as great. Halving ΔT halves the rate: 4 × ½ = 2.
A student who puts the area underneath and the length on top picks this: (1/4) × (1/2) = 1/8. In Q/Δt = kAΔT/L the area is in the numerator: a wider rod conducts energy faster.
questions.explain: Q/Δt = kAΔT/L. The cross-sectional area is proportional to the square of the diameter, so doubling the diameter makes the area 4 times as great. Halving ΔT halves the rate: 4 × ½ = 2.
questions.working: Q/Δt = kAΔT/L. A = πd²/4, so d → 2d gives A → 4A; ΔT → ΔT/2; k and L unchanged. Factor = 4 × ½ = 2. (Area ∝ d: 2 × ½ = 1. Area ignored: ½. L/A instead of A/L: ¼ × ½ = ⅛.)

questions.q: A section of brick wall has an area of 4.0 m² and a thickness of 0.10 m. Its inner surface is at 19.0°C and its outer surface is at 3.0°C. The thermal conductivity of the brick is 0.70 W/(m·K). At what rate is energy conducted through this section of wall?
optionWhy: A student who uses the temperature of the warmer surface, 19.0°C, instead of the temperature difference picks this. Conduction depends on the difference between the two surfaces, 16.0 K.
A student who leaves out the area picks this: (0.70 W/(m·K))(16.0 K)/(0.10 m) = 112 W is the rate through each square meter of wall. The section's area, 4.0 m², multiplies it.
A student who adds 273 to the temperature difference picks this. A difference of 16.0°C is a difference of 16.0 K; 273 is added only when converting a temperature.
Q/Δt = kAΔT/L with ΔT = 19.0°C − 3.0°C = 16.0 K: (0.70 W/(m·K))(4.0 m²)(16.0 K)/(0.10 m) = 448 W, or 4.5 × 10² W to two significant figures.
questions.explain: Q/Δt = kAΔT/L with ΔT = 19.0°C − 3.0°C = 16.0 K: (0.70 W/(m·K))(4.0 m²)(16.0 K)/(0.10 m) = 448 W, or 4.5 × 10² W to two significant figures.

questions.q: A hot metal spoon is placed in a cup of cool water, and the cup is sealed inside an insulated container, so that the spoon and the water form an isolated system. What happens to the total entropy of the spoon and the water as they approach a common temperature?
options: It increases, because energy spreads from the spoon into the water.
It stays the same, because no energy enters or leaves the container.
It decreases, because the temperature of the spoon decreases.
It increases at first, then decreases as the temperatures become equal.
optionWhy: Energy transfer from a hot object to a cooler one is irreversible, and the energy becomes more spread out, so by the second law the total entropy of the isolated system increases. It stops increasing when the spoon and the water reach the same temperature.

A student who thinks entropy can change only when energy crosses the system's boundary picks this. No energy leaves the container, but energy spreads within it, from the spoon into the water, and that increases the total entropy.
A student who judges the whole system by the spoon alone picks this. The spoon's entropy does decrease, but the water's increases by more, so the total entropy of the isolated system increases.

A student who thinks entropy is greatest while energy is moving fastest picks this. The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases; it rises until the spoon and the water share one temperature and then stays at that maximum.
questions.explain: Energy transfer from a hot object to a cooler one is irreversible, and the energy becomes more spread out, so by the second law the total entropy of the isolated system increases. It stops increasing when the spoon and the water reach the same temperature.

questions.q: During a process, the entropy of a system decreases. Which of the following must be true?
options: The system was not isolated during the process.
The second law of thermodynamics was violated.
The temperature of the system became lower.
The system moved closer to thermodynamic equilibrium.
optionWhy: The entropy of an isolated system never decreases. A decrease is possible only if the system interacts with its surroundings, with energy transferred out of it, as when a gas is cooled or is compressed while giving energy to its surroundings.

A student who thinks the second law forbids any system's entropy from decreasing picks this. The law applies to isolated systems; a system that exchanges energy with its surroundings can decrease in entropy while the total entropy of system and surroundings does not decrease.

A student who thinks entropy depends only on temperature picks this. The temperature need not fall: a gas compressed slowly at constant temperature, giving energy to its surroundings, decreases in entropy.

A student who thinks equilibrium is an orderly, low-entropy state picks this. Nothing requires it: a gas can be compressed so slowly that it is in equilibrium at every stage, and its entropy still decreases. What a decrease does require is an interaction with the surroundings.
questions.explain: The entropy of an isolated system never decreases. A decrease is possible only if the system interacts with its surroundings, with energy transferred out of it, as when a gas is cooled or is compressed while giving energy to its surroundings.

questions.q: A moving car brakes to a stop. Treat the car, its brakes, the road and the air as an isolated system. Which statement correctly compares the system after the car stops with the system before?
options: The total energy is less, because some was used up in stopping the car.
The total energy is the same, but less of it is available to do work.
The total energy is the same, and all of it is still available to do work.
The total entropy is the same, because the total energy is the same.
optionWhy: A student who thinks energy is used up picks this. The kinetic energy is not destroyed; it becomes internal energy of the brakes, the road and the air, so the total energy of the isolated system is unchanged.

Energy is conserved in the isolated system, so the total is unchanged. But the car's kinetic energy, which could have done work, has spread out as internal energy of the brakes, the road and the air, and it can no longer all be used to do work: the entropy of the system has increased.

A student who thinks conservation of energy keeps all the energy usable picks this. The energy is still there, but spread out as internal energy of many objects it cannot all be gathered back to set the car moving; less of it is available to do work.

A student who thinks entropy is conserved like energy picks this. Braking is irreversible and spreads the energy out, so the total entropy of the isolated system increases while its total energy stays the same.
questions.explain: Energy is conserved in the isolated system, so the total is unchanged. But the car's kinetic energy, which could have done work, has spread out as internal energy of the brakes, the road and the air, and it can no longer all be used to do work: the entropy of the system has increased.

questions.q: A long metal rod is insulated on all sides. At first the rod is at one uniform temperature, except for a short section in the middle that has just been heated. In each numbered graph, the dashed curve shows the temperature T along the rod at that moment as a function of position x. Which graph's solid curve shows the temperature along the rod a short time later?
options: Graph 1
Graph 2
Graph 3
Graph 4
optionWhy: A student who thinks the energy of the hot section is used up picks the graph in which the whole rod returns to its starting temperature. The rod is insulated, so the energy stays in it and spreads out; the parts near the middle must end up warmer than they started.

A student who thinks heat carries its temperature with it picks the graph in which the whole rod reaches the temperature of the hot section. The same energy spread over more of the rod raises each part less; bringing the whole rod to the peak temperature would need far more energy than was supplied.

A student who thinks nothing changes inside an isolated object picks the graph in which the temperature profile stays the same. No energy crosses the insulation, but energy still spreads within the rod from the hot section to the cooler ones.

Energy concentrated in the heated section spreads along the rod: the middle cools and the neighboring sections warm. The rod is insulated, so no energy is lost, and the hump becomes lower and wider rather than disappearing.
questions.explain: Energy concentrated in the heated section spreads along the rod: the middle cools and the neighboring sections warm. The rod is insulated, so no energy is lost, and the hump becomes lower and wider rather than disappearing.
questions.working: The rod is insulated, so its total internal energy is constant; energy spreads from the heated section into the cooler neighboring sections. The peak falls and the hump widens, with the area between the curve and the starting-temperature level (proportional to the energy added) unchanged. The correct graph shows a lower, wider hump.

figure.alt: Four panels numbered 1 to 4 (1 top left, 2 top right, 3 bottom left, 4 bottom right), each a graph of T against position x. In every panel a dashed curve is flat at a low temperature except for a narrow, tall hump in the middle. The solid curve is panel 1, flat along the whole rod at the dashed curve's low level; panel 2, flat along the whole rod at the height of the dashed hump's peak; panel 3, the same narrow, tall hump, lying on the dashed curve; panel 4, a lower, wider hump centered in the same place.

questions.q: A sealed, insulated box is divided by a partition. One side contains a gas, and the other side is evacuated. The partition is removed, and the gas spreads through the box. At which of the following times is the entropy of the gas greatest?
options: Before the partition is removed, while the gas is on one side
While the gas is rushing into the empty side most rapidly
At every time equally, since no energy crosses the walls
After the gas has spread out evenly through all of the box
optionWhy: A student who thinks an even spread is orderly, and so low in entropy, picks this. The confined gas has its energy and matter in a smaller region; spreading through the whole box increases the entropy.

A student who thinks entropy is greatest while things change fastest picks this. The entropy is still increasing while the gas rushes in; it is greatest once the gas has spread evenly and stopped changing.
A student who thinks entropy changes only when energy crosses the boundary picks this. No energy enters or leaves the box, but the gas spreads within it, and that increases its entropy.

The gas is an isolated system that moves toward equilibrium, and its entropy increases as it spreads. The entropy reaches its maximum when the gas is in equilibrium, spread evenly through the whole box, and stays there.
questions.explain: The gas is an isolated system that moves toward equilibrium, and its entropy increases as it spreads. The entropy reaches its maximum when the gas is in equilibrium, spread evenly through the whole box, and stays there.
